subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
exam_relevance: 10-12 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct definition of an array?

options.A: A collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations
options.B: A collection of elements accessed using an index
options.C: A linear data structure with fixed size
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three—same type, index-based access, fixed-size linear structure—are correct properties of an array. D is correct.

questions.question: In a one-dimensional array A[0..n-1] stored in row-major order, the address of element A[i] is given by:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Address of A[i] = Base + (i - LB) × element_size. When LB=0, it simplifies to Base + i × size.

questions.question: For a 2D array A[1..m][1..n] stored in row-major order, the address of element A[i][j] is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Row-major: A[i][j] = Base + [(i-1)*n + (j-1)] * size. Each row has n elements; i-1 full rows precede row i.

questions.question: For a 2D array A[1..m][1..n] stored in column-major order, the address of element A[i][j] is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Column-major: A[i][j] = Base + [(j-1)*m + (i-1)] * size. Each column has m elements; j-1 full cols precede col j.

questions.question: A sparse matrix is defined as a matrix in which:

options.A: The number of non-zero elements exceeds the number of zero elements
options.B: The number of zero elements is greater than half of the total number of elements
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A sparse matrix has more than half its elements as zeros (zeros > total/2). This matches BPSC TRE 1.0 paper answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is an efficient way to store a sparse matrix?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Both triplet (row, col, value) and linked list representations efficiently store only non-zero elements of a sparse matrix.

questions.question: The time complexity of accessing an element at index i in a 1D array is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Array access by index is O(1) — constant time — because the address is computed directly using base + offset formula.

questions.question: If an array A[5..25] is stored with each element taking 4 bytes and base address 1000, then address of A[15] in row-major order is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: Which of the following operations on an array has worst-case time complexity O(n)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Insertion/deletion at beginning requires shifting n elements O(n). Searching unsorted array is also O(n) linear search.

questions.question: A 2D array B[1..8][1..9] is stored in column-major order. Base address = 100, each element = 2 bytes. Address of B[5][4] is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: Which of the following data structure follows Last In First Out (LIFO) principle?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Stack uses LIFO: last element pushed is first to be popped. Queue uses FIFO. Linked list has no such restriction.

questions.question: Which of the following are applications of a stack?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three—expression conversion, recursion/function calls, and undo/redo—are classic stack applications.

questions.question: The operation that removes an element from the top of a stack is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pop removes the top element. Push adds to top. Peek/Top reads without removing. Only Pop removes from top.

questions.question: Convert infix expression A+B*C to postfix:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: * has higher precedence than +. So B*C evaluates first giving BC*. Then A+BC* → ABC*+. Postfix: ABC*+

questions.question: Convert infix expression (A+B)*(C-D) to postfix:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Postfix of (A+B) is AB+, postfix of (C-D) is CD-. Combined with *: AB+CD-*.

questions.question: Evaluate the postfix expression: 5 3 2 * + using a stack:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Push 5, push 3, push 2. Op *: pop 2,3 → 3*2=6, push 6. Op +: pop 6,5 → 5+6=11, push 11. Result=11.

questions.question: If elements are pushed onto a stack in the order A, B, C, D and then popped, what is the order of output?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LIFO: last in = first out. Push order A,B,C,D → pop order D,C,B,A.

questions.question: What condition indicates an overflow in a stack?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Stack overflow occurs when top reaches the maximum index (MAX_SIZE - 1). top == -1 indicates underflow (empty stack).

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct order of precedence (highest to lowest) for operators in infix-to-postfix conversion?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Operator precedence: ^ (exponent) > * / (multiply/divide) > + - (add/subtract). Option A is correct.

questions.question: Convert postfix expression AB+C* to infix:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: AB+ → (A+B). Then (A+B)C* → (A+B)*C. Postfix AB+C* equals infix (A+B)*C.

questions.question: Evaluate postfix: 2 3 1 * + 9 - using a stack. The result is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: Which data structure is used to check balanced parentheses in an expression?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Stack is used: push opening brackets, pop when closing bracket found, check if match. If stack empty at end → balanced.

questions.question: Which of the following data structure follows First In First Out (FIFO) principle?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Queue follows FIFO: first element inserted is first to be removed. Stack is LIFO. Priority Queue orders by priority.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are true about a Queue data structure?

options.B: It is a linear data structure
options.C: Elements are inserted at rear and deleted from front
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true about Queue. BPSC TRE 2.0 had this exact pattern — answer D (More than one of the above).

questions.question: In a circular queue of size n, the queue is full when:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Circular queue is full when (rear+1)%n == front. This distinguishes full from empty (front == rear).

questions.question: The operation to add an element to a queue is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Enqueue (or offer in Java) adds an element to the rear of a queue. Push is for stacks. Enqueue is the standard term.

questions.question: A priority queue is a queue in which:

options.A: Elements are inserted and removed based on their priority
options.B: Higher priority elements are dequeued before lower priority elements
options.C: Elements may not follow strict FIFO order
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three statements are true for a priority queue. Elements with higher priority are served first regardless of arrival order.

questions.question: A deque (Double-Ended Queue) allows insertion and deletion:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Deque supports insert/delete at BOTH ends (front and rear), making it more flexible than a standard queue or stack.

questions.question: Which of the following is a real-world application of Queue?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CPU scheduling, printer spooling, and BFS all use Queue. All three are standard queue applications.

questions.question: In BPSC TRE paper, a function fun(int x){ q1.offer(x); } is defined. The functionality is best described as:

options.A: Stack push via queue (Queue as Stack)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: offer() inserts at rear. If you pop from front in reverse sequence, it mimics stack behavior. TRE 1.0 answer: B.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of a simple linear queue over a circular queue?

options.A: Linear queue wastes memory due to shifting of front pointer
options.B: Linear queue is slower for insertion
options.C: Linear queue cannot handle multiple data types
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In linear queue, dequeue moves front forward, leaving unused memory. Circular queue reuses that space.

questions.question: If a circular queue has size 6 (indices 0-5), front=2, rear=5, how many elements does it currently contain?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Elements = (rear - front + size) % size + 1 = (5-2+6)%6+1 = 9%6+1 = 3+1 = 4 elements.

questions.question: Which of the following is/are advantages of a linked list over an array?

options.A: Dynamic memory allocation (size not fixed at compile time)
options.B: Efficient insertion and deletion without shifting
options.C: No memory wastage due to pre-allocation
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are advantages of linked list over array: dynamic size, O(1) insertion/deletion at known position, no pre-allocation waste.

questions.question: In a singly linked list, each node contains:

options.A: Data and a pointer to the next node
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Singly linked list node has: data field + one next pointer. Doubly linked list has prev and next pointers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about a doubly linked list?

options.A: It allows traversal in both directions
options.B: Each node has two pointers: prev and next
options.C: Implementation of doubly linked list is simpler than singly linked list
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Doubly linked list is more complex than singly (two pointers per node). Option C is false. BPSC TRE 1.0 paper answer.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the beginning of a singly linked list?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Inserting at head: create node, point its next to current head, update head pointer. Only 3 steps — O(1).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching for an element in an unsorted singly linked list?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In an unsorted linked list, we must traverse all nodes in worst case to find an element: O(n) linear time.

questions.question: A circular linked list is one in which:

options.A: The last node points to the first node
options.B: There is no NULL pointer at the end
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true: last node→first (no NULL), and traversal loops indefinitely without a termination check.

questions.question: In a linked list, after performing the operations: insert(10), insert(20), insert(30), delete(20), insert(40), insert(15), the final list from head to tail is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Insert at tail: 10→20→30. Delete 20: 10→30. Insert 40: 10→30→40. Insert 15: 10→30→40→15. TRE 1.0 answer: C mapped to 10 30 40 15.

questions.question: Which pointer is maintained in a singly linked list to delete the last node efficiently?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: To delete last node, we need prev pointer (second-last node) to set its next = NULL. Traversal to second-last: O(n).

questions.question: Which of the following operation(s) on a doubly linked list is/are O(1) given a pointer to the node?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Doubly linked list: deletion, insertion before/after a given node are all O(1) using prev/next pointers — no traversal needed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a linked list compared to an array?

options.A: Random access is not possible (sequential access only)
options.C: Traversal is slower due to non-contiguous memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Linked list drawbacks: no random access (must traverse), extra pointer memory, non-contiguous memory causes cache misses.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of a singly linked list with n elements?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A singly linked list with n nodes stores n data elements + n pointers = O(n) space.

questions.question: To reverse a singly linked list, the minimum number of pointers needed is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Reversing iteratively needs 3 pointers: prev, current, next. prev=NULL, iterate: save next, link curr→prev, move prev=curr, curr=next.

questions.question: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Binary tree: every node has at most 2 children, called left child and right child.

questions.question: In a full binary tree, every node has:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Full binary tree: every node has either 0 (leaf) or exactly 2 children. No node has exactly 1 child.

questions.question: A perfect binary tree of height h has how many nodes?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Perfect binary tree of height h (root at level 0, leaves at level h): total nodes = 2^(h+1) - 1. E.g. h=2: 7 nodes.

questions.question: The maximum number of nodes at level l of a binary tree is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: At level l (root at level 0), maximum nodes = 2^l. Level 0: 1 node, Level 1: 2 nodes, Level 2: 4 nodes.

questions.question: In-order traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In-order: Left → Root → Right (LNR). Pre-order: Root→Left→Right (NLR). Post-order: Left→Right→Root (LRN).

questions.question: Pre-order traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pre-order: Root → Left → Right (NLR). It visits root first before recursing into subtrees.

questions.question: Post-order traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Post-order: Left → Right → Root (LRN). Root is visited last. Used for deleting a tree or evaluating expression trees.

questions.question: In a balanced binary tree (AVL tree), the height difference between left and right subtrees of any node is at most:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: AVL tree property: |height(left) - height(right)| ≤ 1 for every node. BPSC TRE 3.0 answer: B (at most 1).

questions.question: For a binary tree with n nodes, what is the minimum possible height?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Minimum height of a binary tree with n nodes is ⌊log₂n⌋ (achieved by complete binary tree).

questions.question: If a binary tree has n leaf nodes, how many non-leaf nodes does a full binary tree with these leaves have?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Full binary tree property: if leaf nodes = n, then internal (non-leaf) nodes = n - 1. Total nodes = 2n - 1.

questions.question: What traversal of a binary tree gives nodes in sorted order when applied to a Binary Search Tree?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In-order traversal (Left→Root→Right) of a BST visits nodes in ascending sorted order due to BST property.

questions.question: Given in-order: D B E A F C G and pre-order: A B D E C F G, the root of the right subtree is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Pre-order first = A (root). In-order: left of A = {D,B,E}, right of A = {F,C,G}. Next in pre-order after A is B (left subtree root), then C (right subtree root).

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree (BST), for any node N:

options.A: All nodes in the left subtree have values less than N
options.B: All nodes in the right subtree have values greater than N
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true BST properties: left<root, right>root, and in-order gives ascending sorted output.

questions.question: The worst-case time complexity of search in a Binary Search Tree is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Worst case BST search is O(n) when tree is skewed (degenerate/linear). Average case is O(log n) for balanced BST.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about a Binary Search Tree?

options.B: BST supports searching in O(log n) for balanced trees
options.C: BST guarantees O(log n) search in all cases
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Both A and C are false/debatable: standard BST doesn't allow duplicates, and BST doesn't guarantee O(log n) if unbalanced.

questions.question: The preorder traversal of a BST is: 15, 10, 12, 11, 20, 18, 16, 19. What is the postorder traversal?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Build BST from preorder 15,10,12,11,20,18,16,19. Postorder (LRN): 11,12,10,16,19,18,20,15. BPSC TRE 3.0 answer: B (same value).

questions.question: What is the in-order traversal of the BST with preorder: 15, 10, 12, 11, 20, 18, 16, 19?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In-order of a BST always gives sorted ascending order: 10,11,12,15,16,18,19,20.

questions.question: When deleting a node with two children from a BST, it is typically replaced by:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BST deletion with two children: replace node value with in-order predecessor (max of left) or in-order successor (min of right).

questions.question: The minimum value in a BST is found at:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BST property: smaller values go left. The minimum is always at the leftmost node (keep going left until no left child).

questions.question: If you insert keys 5, 3, 7, 1, 4 into an empty BST, the root is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: First inserted key becomes root. Keys inserted: 5 (root), 3 (left of 5), 7 (right of 5), 1 (left of 3), 4 (right of 3). Root = 5.

questions.question: If you insert keys 5, 3, 7, 1, 4 into an empty BST, what is the in-order traversal?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In-order of BST is always sorted ascending: 1, 3, 4, 5, 7.

questions.question: Which traversal of a BST gives nodes in descending order?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Reverse in-order (Right→Root→Left) of a BST visits nodes in descending sorted order.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Bubble Sort?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Bubble Sort worst case: O(n²) — occurs when array is reverse sorted. Requires n*(n-1)/2 comparisons.

questions.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms has the best average-case time complexity?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Merge Sort: O(n log n) average case. Bubble and Selection Sort are O(n²). Merge Sort is significantly better for large n.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is stable and uses divide-and-conquer?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Merge Sort is stable (preserves relative order of equal elements) and uses divide-and-conquer. Quick Sort is not stable.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Quick Sort worst case: O(n²) — occurs when pivot is always smallest or largest (sorted/reverse sorted array).

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is best suited for sorting a nearly sorted array?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Insertion Sort is O(n) for nearly sorted arrays (best case), making it ideal. Each element needs few comparisons.

questions.question: Heap Sort has what time complexity in all cases?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Heap Sort: O(n log n) in best, average, AND worst case. It's not affected by input order, unlike Quick Sort.

questions.question: Selection Sort works by:

options.B: Finding the minimum element and placing it at the correct position
options.C: Swapping adjacent elements if they are in wrong order
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Selection Sort: repeatedly find minimum from unsorted part and swap to correct position. O(n²) comparisons always.

questions.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms requires O(n) auxiliary space?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Merge Sort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step. Heap Sort and Insertion Sort are O(1) in-place.

questions.question: After one pass of Bubble Sort on array [5, 3, 1, 4, 2], the array becomes:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT stable?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Selection Sort is NOT stable — equal elements may be reordered. Bubble Sort and Insertion Sort are stable algorithms.

questions.question: The best-case time complexity of Bubble Sort is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Optimized Bubble Sort best case = O(n) for already sorted array — only one pass needed with no swaps.

questions.question: Quick Sort with median-of-three pivot selection has which time complexity?

options.A: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
options.C: O(n log n) in all cases
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Even with median-of-three, Quick Sort remains O(n log n) average and O(n²) worst case. Randomized pivot helps but doesn't eliminate worst case.

questions.question: Linear Search has what time complexity in the worst case?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Linear Search worst case: O(n) — must check every element when target is last or not present.

questions.question: Binary Search requires that the array must be:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Binary Search works ONLY on a sorted array. It compares mid element and eliminates half, giving O(log n) time.

questions.question: Binary Search has worst-case time complexity of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Binary Search: each step halves the search space. After k steps, 2^k = n, so k = log₂n. Worst case = O(log n).

questions.question: In Binary Search on array of 16 elements, maximum number of comparisons in worst case is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Binary Search on 16 elements: log₂(16)+1 = 4+1 = 5 comparisons worst case.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Linear Search?

options.A: It works on both sorted and unsorted arrays
options.B: It has O(n) worst-case time complexity
options.C: Its best case is O(1) when element is first
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three are true: Linear Search works on any array, worst case O(n), best case O(1) if target is first.

questions.question: For Binary Search on a sorted array [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56], the number of comparisons to find element 23 is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Step1: mid=index3=12 (not 23, go right). Step2: mid=index5=23? Wait, mid of [16,23,38,56]=index5=23. Comparison 1:12≠23, 2:23=23. Actually 2 comparisons.

questions.question: Which data structure is used for Breadth-First Search (BFS) traversal of a graph?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BFS uses a Queue to visit all neighbors at current level before moving to the next. DFS uses a Stack (or recursion).

questions.question: Which data structure is used for Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal of a graph?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DFS uses a Stack (or implicit call stack via recursion) to explore as deep as possible before backtracking.

questions.question: An adjacency matrix for a graph with n vertices requires how much space?

options.B: O(n + e) where e is edges
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Adjacency matrix: n×n matrix → O(n²) space regardless of number of edges. Suitable for dense graphs.

questions.question: An adjacency list for a graph with n vertices and e edges requires how much space?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Adjacency list: n lists, total entries = 2e (undirected) or e (directed). Space = O(n + e). Better for sparse graphs.

questions.question: An Eulerian path in a graph is a path that:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Eulerian path traverses every EDGE exactly once. Hamiltonian path visits every VERTEX exactly once.

questions.question: A Hamiltonian path in a graph is a path that:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Hamiltonian path visits every VERTEX exactly once. Eulerian path covers every EDGE exactly once.

questions.question: For an undirected graph to have an Eulerian circuit, every vertex must have:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Eulerian circuit exists if and only if every vertex has even degree (Euler's theorem).

questions.question: In a graph with 5 vertices, the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Max edges in simple undirected graph with n vertices = n*(n-1)/2 = 5*4/2 = 10.

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct order of Big-O complexity from best to worst?

options.A: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²)
options.B: O(log n) < O(1) < O(n) < O(n²) < O(n log n)
options.C: O(1) < O(n) < O(log n) < O(n log n) < O(n²)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Correct order: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²). Constant < logarithmic < linear < linearithmic < quadratic.

questions.question: Big-O notation O(f(n)) represents:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Big-O gives the upper bound — worst-case growth rate. Omega (Ω) = lower bound. Theta (Θ) = tight bound.

questions.question: The time complexity of an algorithm that halves the problem size at each step is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Halving at each step: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n). Binary search is the classic example.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the following nested loop: for i=1 to n: for j=1 to n: print(i,j)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Two nested loops each running n times: n × n = n² total iterations → O(n²) time complexity.

questions.question: Space complexity of recursive binary search with n elements is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Recursive binary search: each call halves the array. Recursion depth = log₂n → O(log n) stack space.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the Theta (Θ) notation?

options.A: Lower bound on the running time
options.B: Upper bound on the running time
options.C: Both upper and lower bounds (tight bound)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Theta (Θ) notation: tight bound — algorithm runs in Θ(f(n)) means it's both O(f(n)) and Ω(f(n)).

questions.question: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n has solution (by Master Theorem):

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Master Theorem: a=2,b=2,f(n)=n. log_b(a)=log₂2=1. f(n)=n=n^1=n^log_b(a). Case 2: T(n)=Θ(n log n).

questions.question: NOT a step in the Divide and Conquer strategy is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: All three—Divide, Conquer, Combine—ARE steps of D&C. No correct answer among A/B/C as 'NOT a step'. BPSC TRE 3.0: E (None).
